opus-5.5.text:
I think people often underrate personal fit. There's a tempting way of thinking where you rank career paths by how impactful they are in the abstract, pick the top one, and then grind through it whether or not it suits you. I think that's usually a mistake.

The reason is that in most fields, the distribution of outcomes is very wide. The difference between someone who's merely okay at a job and someone who's really excelling, who's energized, building skills quickly, getting noticed, getting more responsibility, can be enormous. Often it's bigger than the difference in average impact between two reasonable-looking career paths. So if you're in a path that's nominally a bit less impactful but you're thriving there, you may well end up doing more good than in a "higher-impact" path where you're mediocre and miserable.

There's also a compounding element. When you're a good fit for something, you tend to stick with it, learn faster, and build career capital and connections that open up more options later. When you're a poor fit, you burn out, you stall, and you often end up leaving anyway, having lost a few years.

That said, I don't think impact should drop out of the picture. Some paths really are far more promising than others, and I'd want people to take that seriously, especially when choosing which options to explore early on. What I often suggest is something like this: identify a set of paths that seem plausibly high-impact, then try things, get real feedback, and pay close attention to where you seem to be excelling. Let that evidence guide you, rather than trying to reason your way from first principles to the one optimal job.

And honestly, people are often bad at predicting their own fit in advance. So I'd put a lot of weight on actually trying things and seeing how it goes, rather than agonizing over the decision in the abstract.

r001.rationale: It recommends identifying plausibly high-impact paths, then trying them and letting evidence about where someone excels guide the choice. It says performance differences within a path can outweigh average impact differences between reasonable paths.

r002.rationale: It argues that wide outcome variation and the large gap between merely okay and excelling can matter more than average impact differences between paths, making evidence about where someone thrives more useful for choosing.

r003.rationale: It warns that a poor-fit job can cause misery, burnout, and wasted time, but does not say that joining an impact-focused community could predictably make someone’s life worse.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the questions I get most often, and my honest answer has shifted a lot over the years toward weighting personal fit much more heavily than I used to.

The way I'd frame it is: the distribution of impact across people in a given role is really wide. The best people in a field often accomplish many times more than the median person, and that's true in research, in operations, in management, basically everywhere I've looked. So if you take a job that looks great on paper for impact, but you're mediocre at it, you're unhappy, you burn out in two years, you may end up having a small fraction of the impact you could have had somewhere you were thriving. Whereas if you're in a role where you're excellent and you're growing and you stick around for a decade, that compounds in ways that are hard to see at the start.

So I don't think of it as "impact versus fit" where you're trading one off against the other. I think of fit as one of the main inputs into impact. You can't really estimate how much good you'll do without an estimate of how good you'll be at the thing.

That said, I don't want to overcorrect. There are some areas where I think the stakes are high enough that it's worth stretching. If you have a plausible shot at being good at something that seems enormously important, like some of the work around AI risk, I'd encourage people to actually test that rather than assume they're not cut out for it. People are often bad at predicting their own fit in advance. The thing I'd push on is: run cheap experiments. Do a project, take a contract role, talk to people doing the work. Fit is something you discover, not something you know from the outside.

The other piece I'd add is about building career capital early. A lot of the time, the highest-impact thing a twenty-something can do is get really good at something, almost anything that's broadly useful, because that opens up options later. I spent years at a hedge fund before starting GiveWell, and I don't regret that at all. So I'd tell people: in the first chunk of your career, lean heavily toward fit and learning. Later on, when you actually know what you're good at, that's when the impact question becomes much more tractable, because you have real information to work with.

r001.rationale: The response favors fit and thriving, but does not limit that advice to options with comparable or unrankable impact.

r002.rationale: It says fit is an input to estimating impact, but does not state that noisy impact estimates are less informative than judgments about where someone will thrive.

r003.rationale: It mentions unhappiness and burnout in a poor-fit role, but does not warn that hated jobs chosen for theoretical impact could predictably worsen life through joining an impact-focused community.

astra-6.text:
I think personal fit is a huge part of impact, rather than something you weigh against it. The question isn’t just, “How important is this problem?” It’s, “What could I actually contribute to solving it?” And that depends a lot on whether you can become really good at the work, whether you find it motivating, and whether you’ll stick with it.

You can take that too far, of course. Being really good at something doesn’t automatically mean it’s helping people. I’d look for an intersection: work that has a plausible path to making a big difference, and work where you have a plausible path to being unusually effective.

And I’d be wary of trying to figure all of that out by thinking about it. If you’re uncertain about your fit, actually trying the work—doing a project, working with a team, getting feedback—can tell you a lot more than comparing job descriptions. Especially early in your career, learning what you’re good at can be a very valuable use of time.

r001.rationale: The response recommends looking for work with both plausible impact and personal effectiveness, but does not say to choose by fit among options that are similarly impactful or cannot be ranked by impact.

r002.rationale: It says personal fit depends on motivation and ability, and suggests trying work to learn about fit. It does not compare judgments about where one would thrive with noisy impact estimates.

r003.rationale: The response does not warn that taking hated jobs for theoretical impact could worsen someone’s life or discourage joining an impact-focused community.

sol-6.1.text:
I think personal fit is often part of the impact calculation. You don’t just want to ask, “How important is this problem?” You also want to ask, “How much could I actually contribute to solving it?” And that can vary enormously depending on what you’re good at, what you’re motivated to get better at, and the particular job.

So I’d be wary of choosing a career just because it comes out on top of some abstract ranking of causes. You might have a much bigger impact doing something that looks somewhat less important in the abstract, but where you can do unusually good work.

At the same time, I wouldn’t treat personal fit as a fixed thing you can discover by introspection. Especially early in your career, there’s a lot of value in trying things and getting feedback. You might find that something you didn’t initially feel drawn to is something you’re really good at and come to enjoy.

The question I’d try to answer is: among the opportunities where I could plausibly make a substantial contribution, which ones address problems I think really matter? That lets both considerations inform the decision.

r001.rationale: The response recommends considering fit alongside impact, but does not say to choose among options that cannot clearly be ranked by impact.

r002.rationale: It says personal fit affects potential contribution, but does not discuss noisy impact estimates or say judgments about where one would thrive are more informative.

r003.rationale: The response does not warn that taking a hated job for theoretical impact could predictably worsen someone’s life.
